lines.text: Sl. 40. भङ्गुरवृत्तयः—evanescent or transient by nature. तैरेव
चायं भवः—And wordly life ( is formed ) of them only. कृतम्—
enough with. समाधीयताम्— fix in one place. कामोच्छित्तिवशे—which
is (now) under control on account of desires being uprooted.
स्वधामनि—in its own place or abode, viz. स्वयंप्रकाशे आत्मनि.

r2.note: Some Devanagari readings are difficult to distinguish.

lines.text: Sl. 41. तृणलव०—of as little consequence as a small blade
of grass. यस्मिन्महाशासने—V. l. Some such words as लब्धे or
अधिगते सति should be taken as understood after this locative.
महाशासने—&c.—The knowledge of Brahma as expounded in the
Upanishads; the highest truth taught by them ( the four
Mahávákyas especially ); Rámarshi explains this by परमात्मज्ञाने
( स्फुरिते सति ). Mr. Telang says—“It means whose commands
are great; thus in the Upanishads एतस्य वा अक्षरस्य गार्गि प्रशासने
सूर्याचन्द्रमसौ तिष्ठतः । or भीषास्माद्वातः पवते &c.; the greatness consist-
ing in the great powers which obey those commands.” But
Rámarshi’s sense seems to be more natural. The knowledge of
Brahma is called Mahâs'âsana because it comes authoritatively
from the Vedas, it being the highest truth taught by them.
कोऽपि—indescribable. Cf. विकारः कोऽप्यन्तर्जडयति च तापं च कुरुते,
Utt. नित्योदित—ever existing, steady, permanent. Cf. with
this sl. 70 infra.; Gîta VI. 22.

r3.note: Some Sanskrit and transliteration characters are indistinct.

lines.text: Sl. 42. रम्या सा would be better for symmetry. सामन्त ( सम्य-
न्तः समन्तः border, frontier, तत्र भवः सामन्तः ) means a frontier
king, a tributary prince. विदग्ध—a wise man. सापि राजपरिषद् v l.
involves tautology since सामन्तचक्र has already occurred. उत्सिक्तः—
swollen or puffed up with pride, proud. उद्रिक्त v. l. ( p p. of रिच्
with उद् ) lit. exceeded, overflowed, hence haughty. निवह—a
collection. स्मृतिपथगत—became a matter of memory i. e. history.

r4.note: The divided Sanskrit word and some Sanskrit readings are unclear.

lines.text: Sl. 43. गृहे—used here in a double sense; (1) a house; (2) a
square on a dice-board. तत्र बहवः—( And there are ) many after
him, i. e. many who follow or depend upon him. The last two
lines describe the game at dice in which the god of death and
his wife (the male and female personifications of the principle of
Destruction) are engaged. The world is their dice-board,

r5.note: The Sanskrit phrase on line 2 is indistinct.
